Betty and a male companion, Abel, were offered a little bucket of food at the bottom of a vertical tube, along with two pieces of wire, one straight and one hooked. Abel flew off with the hook. Betty picked up the straight wire, wedged one end, bent it into a hook, and fished out the bucket. on later trials. It looked like insight, a bird solving a new problem by making a tool it had never been taught to make. Fourteen years later, a team led by Christian Rutz complicated the story. Some wild-caught New Caledonian crows, kept briefly in field aviaries, bent straight twigs without needing to, and one of them used Betty's exact wedge-and-pull technique. Either way, the story carries the lesson of this whole episode. Here's the argument. Intelligence has evolved again and again in very different bodies and brains, in birds, in octopuses, in insects, and in simpler forms in cells and collectives. It is a family of solutions to the problems of staying alive, not a ladder with us at the top. And when we study it, we err in both directions. We see minds that are not there, and we miss minds that are. Start with the two errors. In the early 1900s, a horse in Berlin called Clever Hans appeared to do arithmetic, tapping out answers with a hoof. The psychologist Oskar Funxt showed that Hans was reading tiny, involuntary cues in his questioner's posture, which relaxed when he reached the right number. Hans was clever, just not at arithmetic.
